entries.clue: ... deductions processed? (10)

indicators.note: to process something is to work it over into a new form

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

annotation.surface: An accountant's query about whether the deductions have gone through yet.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: a price with its deductions applied has been discounted, and the letters of DEDUCTIONS rework into exactly that word.
annotation.definitionFit: Goods with deductions taken off the price have been discounted.

entries.clue: Author often adjacent to Rice? (4)

blocks.note: a writer of Charlie and the Chocolate Factory
a lentil curry, usually served on the plate next to rice

annotation.surface: A librarian noting that one author's books often sit beside Anne Rice's on the shelf.
annotation.walkthrough: Capital R makes Rice look like the novelist Anne Rice, but the second sense is the plate: dahl (also spelt dal) is a lentil curry served with rice.
annotation.definitionFit: Roald Dahl is one of the best-known authors of children's books.

entries.clue: Rise, being angry (audibly) (4)

indicators.note: tells you to go by how the word is heard, not spelt

blocks.note: sore = angry, as in 'still sore about it'

annotation.surface: Someone's voice rising as they get angry and make it heard.
annotation.walkthrough: SORE for angry is chiefly American but common in crosswords; in non-rhotic British speech SORE and SOAR are identical.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: birds and prices both climb steeply upward in this sense.

entries.clue: Rebuilt hut, barefoot and panting (3,2,6)

indicators.note: something rebuilt is put together again in a new arrangement

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 11 letters

annotation.surface: Someone who has rebuilt a hut with no shoes on and is now panting from the effort.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma makes 'barefoot' look like a description of the builder, but it is simply more letters for the anagram.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom for gasping after exertion, matching the adjective 'panting' in sense and part of speech.

entries.clue: Normally involving: capers; olives (if stoned); eggs – primarily? (7)

annotation.definition: Normally involving: capers; olives (if stoned); eggs – primarily?

indicators.note: take the first, primary, letter of each word

blocks.clueFragment: Normally involving: capers; olives (if stoned); eggs
blocks.note: first letters of Normally, Involving, Capers, Olives, If, Stoned, Eggs

annotation.surface: A recipe card listing what a certain salad normally contains.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: salade niçoise, from Nice, normally contains capers, olives and eggs, so the ingredient list describes the answer while spelling it.
annotation.definitionFit: Niçoise describes a dish in the style of Nice, famously a salad with olives, eggs and capers.

entries.clue: Perhaps lead with a small amount (7)

blocks.note: lead the metal (Pb) is one example of a chemical substance of this kind; 'perhaps' marks the example
a trace, as in 'there's an ___ of truth in it'

annotation.surface: An instruction to start with only a little of something.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lead' wants to be the verb (to go first); here it is the metal, pronounced 'led'.
annotation.definitionFit: Lead is an example of a chemical element, and an element of something is a small trace of it.

entries.clue: Quiet commercial for fish (4)

blocks.note: sh! = be quiet
an ad is a commercial

annotation.surface: A low-key advert selling fish.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Quiet commercial' reads as a soft-sell advert; it is two chunks side by side, a hush and an advert.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: this is a herring-family fish that swims upriver to spawn.

entries.clue: Patriarch and ma identified, in some measure, source of help (10)

indicators.note: only a portion of the words is used

blocks.note: patriarcH AND MA IDENtified

annotation.surface: A genealogist identifying the founding father and mother of a family.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Patriarch and ma' sets up a family tree; the answer runs across the join of the words.
annotation.definitionFit: A handmaiden is a female servant or helper, hence a source of help.

entries.clue: Fruit coming at last, it seems, for romantic evenings (4,6)

indicators.note: take the last letter of each of the following words

blocks.note: a date is a fruit
nigh = approaching, as in 'the end is nigh'
last letters of iT and seemS

annotation.surface: A fruit arriving at last, just in time for some romantic evenings.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Coming at last' reads as one phrase, but it splits: 'coming' is NIGH, and 'at last' works on 'it seems', which looks like mere hedging.
annotation.definitionFit: Date nights are evenings a couple set aside for romance.

entries.clue: Try facial hair, leading to sorrows (10)

blocks.note: a judge hears, or tries, a case
'taches, short for moustaches

annotation.surface: Advice that attempting to grow a beard or moustache only brings sorrow.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Try' looks like 'attempt'; it is the courtroom sense. A 'tache is British slang for a moustache.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the plural: pains of the heart are griefs, so the plural noun matches 'sorrows'.

entries.clue: Insect which, when knocked back, leaves aftertaste (4)

indicators.note: pushed back the way it came, so read right to left

blocks.note: a tang is a sharp lingering taste

annotation.surface: An insect that, swallowed with a drink, leaves a nasty taste.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Knocked back' suggests downing a drink, which suits 'aftertaste'; here it turns TANG around.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the answer is a small two-winged fly, one kind of insect.

entries.clue: Startled Finance with memo describing Director: that's a little novel (2,4,3,3)

indicators.note: startled letters jump into disorder
to describe is also to draw a line around, so the fodder goes round D

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 11 letters
D = director, held inside the fodder

annotation.surface: A finance department alarmed by a memo about its director.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Describing' is used in the geometry sense (describing a circle round something). Steinbeck's Of Mice and Men is a novella, hence 'a little novel'.
annotation.definitionFit: Of Mice and Men is John Steinbeck's short novel, a novella.

entries.clue: Tattered, leathern and characteristic of bygone era (11)

indicators.note: torn to pieces, so the letters are scattered

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 11 letters

annotation.surface: A description of ragged leather clothing from long ago.
annotation.walkthrough: 'And' looks like a link word joining two descriptions; it is part of the fodder. Leathern means made of leather.
annotation.definitionFit: Neanderthal describes the prehistoric era of Neanderthal man, or anything hopelessly old-fashioned.

entries.clue: Cold gâteau spread on a roll (10)

indicators.note: the letters are spread out and rearranged

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters; the accent is ignored

annotation.surface: A cold cake spread onto a bread roll.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On a roll' looks like food; here a roll is a list or register, so something on a roll has been catalogued.
annotation.definitionFit: Something entered on a roll, or list, has been catalogued.

entries.clue: Healthy eating, eg fried onion rings and donuts, did you say? (5,5)

indicators.note: asks about what was spoken, so go by sound

blocks.clueFragment: eg fried onion rings and donuts
blocks.note: onion rings and ring donuts are foods with holes

annotation.surface: A sceptic asking whether fried onion rings and donuts really count as healthy eating.
annotation.walkthrough: The joke is that the least healthy foods are 'hole foods'; said aloud that is WHOLE FOODS, unprocessed healthy eating.
annotation.definitionFit: Whole foods are unrefined, unprocessed foods eaten for health.

entries.clue: Wreathes unopened, rearranged for source of wood (3,4)

indicators.note: without its opening letter
arranged anew, so the remaining letters take a fresh order

blocks.note: WREATHES without its first letter W

annotation.surface: Garlands left unopened and rearranged, with wood as the aim.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Wreathes' looks like a verb (to encircle), but it is just the word to be trimmed; 'for' links fodder to definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by function: ash is a tough timber used for tool handles and bats.

entries.clue: Flirtatious: like a pleasing crossword clue? (7)

blocks.note: playfully provocative, as a flirt is
a good clue is a teaser, puzzling you pleasantly

annotation.surface: A setter's wink that a good clue flirts with the solver.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue describes itself: a pleasing crossword clue is teasing, and this one is.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses are adjectives: playfully provocative in manner, and puzzling in a way that tantalises, as a brain-teaser does.

entries.clue: Alert! Debt changing hands two out of three times (3,4)

indicators.text: changing hands two out of three times
indicators.note: swap R (right hand) for L (left hand) in two of its three places

blocks.note: arrears = money owed

blocks.clueFragment: changing hands two out of three times
blocks.note: ARREARS has three Rs; the first two become L

annotation.surface: A warning that a debt keeps being passed from one owner to another.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Changing hands' sounds like transferring ownership; in crossword terms R and L are right and left hands, and ARREARS has three Rs.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone all ears is alert and listening closely.

entries.clue: Collapse, having lost heart after second misgiving (7)

indicators.note: the middle letter is removed
the collapse word is placed after S

blocks.note: S = second
CRUMPLE without its middle letter M

annotation.surface: Someone collapsing after a second attack of doubt.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue reads Collapse first, but 'after' puts it behind S.
annotation.definitionFit: A scruple is a moral misgiving that holds you back.

entries.clue: Recorded match on the radio, leading to ... beef? (3,4)

indicators.note: radio is heard, not seen, so go by sound

blocks.note: a meter read, or recorded, a figure
a meet is a sporting match

annotation.surface: A match broadcast on the radio that sparks an argument.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Beef' looks like the slang for a quarrel, which suits a match; the question mark flags it as an example of red meat.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example, flagged by the question mark: meat from cattle belongs to the dark-fleshed class alongside lamb and venison.

entries.clue: Rows – in a predecessor of tennis? (7)

blocks.note: rows (rhyming with 'cows') are noisy quarrels, din
an old racquet-and-ball game played against the walls of a court

annotation.surface: Arguments breaking out during an old-fashioned ball game.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rows' could be lines or oarsmen; here it is loud quarrels. Rackets is the game in which squash began, older than lawn tennis.
annotation.definitionFit: Rackets are din and uproar; rackets is also an old court game.

entries.clue: Get some scoff there, Cordelia – with no one knowing (3,3,6)

indicators.note: take only part of the following words

blocks.note: scOFF THERE CORDelia

annotation.surface: Someone urging Cordelia to eat something secretly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Scoff' is British slang for food, and 'some scoff' reads as 'some food'; really 'some' takes a portion of the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Something said off the record is not made public, so no one knows it came from you.

entries.clue: Fictional Captain seeing augury ascending (4)

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading bottom to top

blocks.note: an augury is an omen

annotation.surface: A storybook captain spotting a sign in the sky.
annotation.walkthrough: An augury is a sign of things to come; 'ascending' only works as a reversal because this is a down clue.
annotation.definitionFit: Captain Nemo commands the Nautilus in Jules Verne's novels.

entries.clue: 'Cast-off folksy Everyman' – Editor (4)

blocks.note: Everyman is the setter, i.e. ME; in folksy speech 'us' means me ('give us a kiss')
ed. = editor

annotation.surface: A newspaper editor quoting a dismissive description of the paper's own setter.
annotation.walkthrough: The setter's pen name stands for ME, and folksy dialect turns that into US.
annotation.definitionFit: Cast-off clothes are used, second-hand ones.

entries.clue: Buffoon's regularly seen 'ETs' vehicles' (4)

indicators.note: only letters at regular intervals are visible

blocks.note: bUfFoOnS: the even letters

annotation.surface: A clown who keeps claiming to have spotted alien spacecraft.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in 'Buffoon's' is just part of the surface; the S it attaches supplies the final letter.
annotation.definitionFit: UFOs are the craft extraterrestrials are supposed to fly.

entries.clue: Absent-minded father of the bride might be this shocked (10)

annotation.definition2: Absent-minded father of the bride might be this

blocks.clueFragment: Absent-minded father of the bride might be this
blocks.note: the bride's father gives the wedding toast; forget it and he is without his address
too shocked to speak

annotation.surface: A father of the bride so stunned he forgets his speech.
annotation.walkthrough: At a British wedding the bride's father traditionally gives a speech, so a forgetful one is left without one, SPEECH-LESS.
annotation.definitionFit: Both are adjectives: shocked into silence, and literally lacking the expected wedding address.

entries.clue: Add powder. Remove powder (4)

blocks.note: sprinkle, as with icing sugar on a cake
wipe clean, as with a cloth on a shelf

annotation.surface: Two contradictory instructions, one after the other.
annotation.walkthrough: The same verb means opposite things: you dust a cake with icing sugar, and you dust a mantelpiece to clean it.
annotation.definitionFit: Dust means both to sprinkle with powder and to clear of it.

entries.clue: Pop perhaps wanting a bit of waffle (6,4)

blocks.note: 'pop' is a word that goes with weasel, as in the rhyme 'Pop goes the weasel'
an evasive, deliberately vague term

annotation.surface: Someone's dad fancying a waffle.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pop' looks like father or a fizzy drink; think of the nursery rhyme 'Pop goes the weasel', which makes it a weasel's word.
annotation.definitionFit: A weasel word is a vague, slippery term used to evade, a bit of waffle.
